title: Architectures: Memory

sentences.text: So today, we're going to be doing our last of this mini series on machine learning architectures or deep learning architectures.
So previously, we talked about CNNs, GNNs, things like transformers.
And today, we're going to be introducing the concepts of memory and sequence modeling.
And we have seen different types of ways to model sequences in the past.
We talked about 3D CNNs that have time or transformers that have a sense of time.
But today, we're going to be introducing a new class of types of models that handle memory and sequences in a different way.
And this will be the first class of architectures that we talk about that's actually, quote, unquote, Turing complete.
So this is actually the most general framework of the architectures that we're going to be introducing.
So we'll first motivate again why we think we might want to model sequences, model something like time or order.
And then we'll talk about how we might use CNNs for sequences.
We'll introduce the concept of an RNN, or Recurrent Neural Network.
And then we'll go through an extension or a specific subset of RNNs called LSTMs.
That stands for Long Short-Term Memory.
And these actually seek to specifically avoid one of the common issues with RNNs, which is forgetting.
And then we'll introduce the idea of sequence modeling and long memory and start talking about some things like autoregression.

What color is the chair?

We rely on context and information.

There's these complex relationships between the actions.
And then things like predicting she's going to fall, that she believes that the chair is there, why she believes that the chair is there, whether you guys are going to laugh at it.

And so all of this is really very complex and nuanced understanding about the scenes, the objects, and things like intent, which we could argue about whether these machine learning models that model sequences are really getting at understanding things like human intent.
But they do start to try to get at this sense of what is going to happen next.
So sequences can be a lot of things.

We're extending this fourth temporal dimension, because we have multiple inputs of red, green, and blue for each of those dimensions.
And then time just becomes another spatial dimension in that tensor.
So now, you have a 4D tensor instead of a 2D tensor.
And so now, when we're thinking about how we might actually try to represent time, there's different ways that we can think about capturing time within this cube.
And one interesting way that you can model temporal structure can be something like taking a slice through that space-time cube.

What are these stripes likely to be?
People walking.
Yeah, people walking, and walking at different angles to the camera or with different trajectories or different speeds.
Or you could also think about taking a vertical slice through time.
So now, this is showing, for a given position horizontally or vertically in the frame, who is going through that position first.
Interestingly, even from a very long time ago, they started modeling images like this for the Olympics when they were trying to figure out who was the first person to go across the finish line.
If you take the finish line, and you make that a single pixel element, you can see exactly what pixel crosses first, and that represents the person who won the race.
And so there's lots of different ways you can think about representing or modeling time.
And then if you actually want to think about how you do convolutions in time, if we take a very simple 1D perspective of this-- so now, imagine we're just talking about this scalar perspective.
Then, what you would do is you would, similar to before, learn some weight matrix over some given fixed time window.

So instead of before, where we took an image or something, and we would run this across the image in these different patches, and then you were constrained by the structure of the image, here actually, now, you can run this in time.

Now, you could slide that, and you could slide it arbitrarily long.

I mean, they're only constrained by the length of your input sequence.

And if you're doing this, then what we discover both empirically-- and also it kind of makes sense intuitively-- is that as that time sequence becomes arbitrarily long, it's hard for our memories of what happened at the beginning of the sequence to persist.

And so this type of identification with the context of what you've seen in the past from the same, for example, sequence is really the intuition or the motivation behind the development of what we call recurrent neural networks, so these RNNs.
So transformers, CNNs, everything so far mostly had of fixed window in time.
There was transformers these days-- we can talk about that context window is getting very, very large, but it's still fixed.

You get some value.

So here, if we want to look at this in a little bit more detail, again, just thinking of everything as scalars just because it's really easy to visualize this way.

And the next hidden state-- so now, we have our inputs running through some model to get some hidden state.
And then we send this output, and we also send that hidden state one time step forward.

So here, it's as you're kind of running this through, what we do is we say your next hidden state is represented by some function f that will depend on the previous hidden state and the current input.
And then that f, that function, that's shared over time.

We have a cycle.

So now, what you're learning is you're learning u, which is mapping your input to the next point.
You're learning some v that's mapping your previous hidden state in as well, and you combine them.

So if I got rid of W here, what would this be called-- if I got rid of the kind of recurrence dimension, if we were just looking at that mapping between the input and the output?

What do we need to keep?

as far as you want to unroll.

increase the time window, is it then harder to predict if you only use a couple of inputs at inference time?

key_points.text: The new class of architectures being introduced is Turing complete, representing a general framework for handling memory and sequences.
Computer vision models can identify objects and attributes from a single frame.
Understanding complex relationships, predicting future actions, and grasping human intent requires temporal context and sequence information.

key_terms.definition: Sequence modeling is the process of modeling data that possesses an inherent order or temporal structure, such as time or order. This approach allows models to handle information that unfolds over a series of steps.
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a specific subset of Recurrent Neural Networks. LSTMs are designed to specifically avoid the common issue of forgetting that is present in standard RNNs.

segments.subgoal: Explain how convolutional networks can model temporal data and perform convolutions in time

key_points.text: Sequences can represent various data types, including language, audio, and video.
CNNs can be extended into a 4D space-time cube, treating time as another spatial dimension.
Temporal structure can be modeled by taking slices (horizontal or vertical) through the space-time cube.
Convolutions in time function as sequence-to-sequence models and are not constrained by the structure of an image.

key_terms.definition: Sequence is an ordered collection of data points that can represent various types of information. These sequences include words in language, pictures in a video, or audio signals.

Space-time cube is a four-dimensional tensor created by extending convolutional neural networks (CNNs) into the space-time dimension. This structure allows for the representation of data that includes spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension.

Convolutions in time are a method where a weight matrix is learned over a fixed time window, similar to standard convolutions. This allows the model to process sequences by taking input from multiple positions in the sequence and generating an output position.

segments.subgoal: Explain the limitations of fixed-window convolutions and the motivation for memory units

key_points.text: As time sequences become arbitrarily long, standard convolutional approaches struggle to maintain memory of events that occurred at the beginning of the sequence.
Fixed time windows in a convolutional approach only provide local information and do not inherently contain inputs from the beginning of the sequence.
To overcome the limitations of fixed windows, models must capture context and be able to remember what was seen in the past.
The need to identify objects based on context from past observations is the primary motivation behind the development of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

key_terms.definition: Temporal convolution is a type of convolution that processes input data across a time dimension, utilizing the same weight matrix across the entire sequence.
Memory unit is a component that provides context by storing and giving information about what has been seen in the past of a sequence.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a type of network developed to capture context by remembering information from the past of a sequence.

segments.subgoal: Define the structure and mathematical components of a recurrent neural network

key_points.text: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) overcome the fixed window limitation of models like CNNs and Transformers by allowing infinite context through memory.
The core mechanism of an RNN involves using a hidden unit to take the current input and the memory from the past to predict the output and update the memory.
The functions that govern the hidden state and the output prediction are shared across all time steps.
Because of the feedback loop from the hidden state to itself, RNNs are not a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

segments.subgoal: Explain how backpropagation is applied to networks with loops by truncating the time window

key_points.text: Backpropagation is intended for feedforward networks (DAGs), but recurrent networks contain loops.
To apply backprop to a network with loops, the network is unrolled over a fixed time window, which converts it into a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
Truncating the time window limits the model's ability to learn information from very far back in time.
The size of the fixed time window is a hyperparameter that can be tuned or informed by domain knowledge.

key_terms.definition: Backpropagation is the method used to calculate gradients during training, which is traditionally intended for feedforward networks. It allows the network to learn by propagating error signals backward through the structure.

Fixed time window is a predetermined duration during training that the model is configured to propagate back through. This window allows the recurrent network to be unrolled into a structure suitable for backpropagation.
Unroll is the process of expanding a recurrent network over a specific time window. This process transforms the network, which originally contained loops, into a directed acyclic graph.
Directed acyclic graph is a network structure resulting from unrolling a recurrent process, which prevents the infinite loops that would otherwise exist.

segments.subgoal: Explain backpropagation through shared parameters in sequence models

key_points.text: When unrolling a sequence model, the weights (W's) that map hidden states forward through time are shared across all time steps.
Backpropagation over shared parameters is equivalent to calculating gradients over a branching structure in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
When calculating the gradient for a shared parameter, the gradients from every instance where that parameter occurs must be summed up.
In frameworks like PyTorch, autograd handles the summing of gradients automatically, provided that deep copies of variables are avoided.

key_terms.definition: Gradient descent is the method used to optimize a model by learning how to change parameters (W, U, and V) so that the sum of the loss over a sequence is minimized.

Directed acyclic graph is a network structure where information flows in a specific direction and contains no loops, which allows shared parameters to create a branching structure. When calculating gradients over this structure, the gradients for a specific parameter are summed for every time that parameter occurs in the network.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how recurrence leads to vanishing and exploding gradients in RNNs

key_points.text: RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because the required memory size grows non-parametrically with the sequence length.
The recurrence relationship causes the weight matrix to be raised to the power of the time step (W^N).
This exponential relationship leads to vanishing gradients (small weights go to 0) or exploding gradients (large weights go to infinity).
Vanishing gradients correspond to old memories being forgotten, while exploding gradients correspond to unstable training.

key_terms.definition: Markov assumption dictates that the future hidden state depends solely on the immediate preceding hidden state. This constraint is what allows Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to be called recurrent, even though they theoretically model dependencies over long chains.
Recurrent describes a model where the hidden state depends only on the immediate hidden state from the previous step. This structure allows the model to process sequences of data.
Vanishing gradients occur when the gradients become extremely small during training. This issue often results in old observations being forgotten by the network.
Exploding gradients occur when the gradients become extremely large during training. This condition leads to unstable training and is undesirable for model performance.

segments.subgoal: Explain the mechanism and components of LSTM memory control

key_points.text: LSTMs were introduced to address the vanishing gradient problem inherent in standard RNNs.
LSTMs utilize a cell state (C), which functions like a memory tape, to store information that is modulated by internal gates.
The forget and input gates use sigmoid functions, which are bounded between 0 and 1, to explicitly control what information is retained or added to the cell state.
The gating functionality and the default identity update prevent the exponential growth or decay of gradients, mitigating vanishing and exploding gradient issues.

key_terms.definition: Cell state is a new component introduced in an LSTM that functions like the hidden tape in a Turing machine. This state is modulated by the mechanisms that decide what information to forget and what information to add.

Gating functionality is the mechanism provided by multiplicative updates to the cell state, allowing the model to explicitly learn what information to remember and what information to forget. This functionality is provided by components that decide what to save and what to delete.
Sigmoid function is a non-linearity used in the LSTM that is bounded between 0 and 1. This bounding allows the function to map large values to 1 and small values to 0.

Identity is the default behavior of the LSTM, which is similar to a skipped or residual connection in a ResNet. This allows the model to potentially learn to simply send the same information forward without modification.

The probability of a sequence is modeled by factorizing the joint distribution into a product of conditional probabilities (,).
Next-word prediction can be treated as a multi-class classification problem using a softmax function (,).

key_terms.definition: Autoregressive model is a type of sequence model where the system predicts the next element in a sequence based on the elements that came before it. The prediction made at one time step is then fed back into the model as input for predicting the subsequent element.

Softmax is a function that takes an input and transforms it into a probability distribution. This function ensures that the outputs are non-negative and sum up to one.

Next-word classifier is a model designed to predict the most likely word that follows a given sequence of words. This model treats the sequence prediction task as a multi-class classification problem.

segments.subgoal: Compare autoregressive generation methods with memory-based and attention architectures

key_points.text: During training, teacher forcing is often used in sequence generation to condition each next word prediction on the ground-truth preceding words, rather than the model's own prediction.
Beam search is an algorithm used in autoregressive modeling to explore multiple likely paths (top k) and select the sequence with the highest overall probability.
Modern language modeling often utilizes Transformers, which allow for sharing information across all time steps simultaneously, instead of relying solely on sequential models.
Memory networks allow every time step to maintain a memory unit, enabling direct linking of old memories to future predictions without constrained sequential passing.

key_terms.definition: Byte pairs are a tokenization method that represents words using pairs of characters. These tokens are frequently used even in the largest scale language models.

Teacher forcing is a training technique where the model is conditioned on the ground-truth preceding words, even if the model predicts an incorrect word at a given time step. This prevents the model from penalizing itself for mistakes made after the initial error.

Autoregressive modeling is a process where the model predicts the next element in a sequence one step at a time. This prediction is conditioned on the previous elements that have already been generated.

Beam search is a decoding technique that allows the model to choose the top k most likely candidates at each step. It fills out a tree of possibilities and selects the path that scores best overall, representing the model's confidence in the entire sequence.

A memory unit is a concept where every single time step is allowed to maintain a memory representation. This allows for direct linking of old memories to future predictions, rather than strictly passing information forward in a constrained way.

key_points.text: Standard self-attention has a quadratic computational complexity ($O(N^2)$) with respect to sequence length $N$.
Sparsification methods, such as Reformer and Performer, reduce attention complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$ or $O(N \log N)$ using low-rank approximation.
Longformer and Transformer XL increase context windows by deconstructing attention into local and global attention.
Retrieval-enhanced transformers use external knowledge bases to enforce factual validity and prevent hallucinations.

key_terms.definition: Recurrence is a method for modeling arbitrarily long sequences where recurrent weights are shared over time, passing forward information across a time window. This process can be implemented using vanilla recursion or more complex structures like an LSTM.

Convolution is a method for modeling arbitrarily long sequences using a fixed set of convolution weights that are shared over time. However, this method cannot see anything outside of the defined time window of that convolution.

Attention is a mechanism where weights are dynamically determined as a function of the data, which makes the way information is kept dependent on the inputs. This flexibility allows for highly adaptable sequence modeling.
Self-attention is a computation where the similarity of the entire sequence is calculated against itself. This process requires an $N^2$ computation, where $N$ is the length of the sequence.

Retrieval enhanced transformers is an architecture that decomposes a large language model into a lightweight language model and a memory bank. This setup allows the model to perform fact lookup in a database, helping to enforce factual validity.

open_questions.prompt: Explain how an autoregressive model works to generate a sequence of text.
open_questions.reference_answer: An autoregressive model works by continually predicting what comes next in a sequence. The process involves taking the current input, asking the predictor for the next element, and then adding that prediction back into the input for the subsequent step. This loop allows the model to generate text word by word. Essentially, the model is learning the conditional probability of the next word given all the previous words. This is often implemented using a next-word classifier and a softmax function to output a probability distribution over possible next words.

open_questions.prompt: Your friend missed the lecture on Sequence Generation and Memory Architectures. Explain the limitations of traditional autoregressive models and how modern approaches like memory units and attention address the challenge of long-range dependencies.
open_questions.reference_answer: Traditional autoregressive modeling, such as using LSTMs, predicts one word at a time, and if a mistake is made, it can take the model down a path where it makes many subsequent errors. To overcome this, modern architectures propose giving every single time step a memory unit, allowing the model to keep memories from every point in time. Instead of sending information forward in a constrained way, methods like temporal convolutions, attention, and transformers directly link old memories to future predictions. This ability to share information across all temperatures indeterminately is key to handling long-range dependencies effectively.

open_questions.prompt: Imagine a classmate missed the lecture on Architectures: Memory. Explain the main idea of LSTMs and how they solve the vanishing gradient problem in simple terms.
open_questions.reference_answer: LSTMs were introduced primarily to deal with the vanishing gradient problem. They are designed so that the default behavior is to not forget, which is similar to having a hidden tape in a Turing machine. The core of the LSTM is the cell state (C), which is modulated by gates that decide what to save and what to delete. Crucially, the model uses multiplicative relationships, allowing the cell state to maintain an identity function by default. This structure prevents the exponential decay that causes the vanishing gradient issue.
